headline: Mostly dry now; isolated southwest storms later Thursday.
summary:
The latest MSLP charts show a slack pressure pattern across Britain, with a weak low over Scotland earlier replaced by a weak ridge extending from highs to the west of Ireland and the North Sea. Compared with yesterday afternoon, the synoptic driver has become less cyclonic and more weakly anticyclonic, leaving England and Wales with little organised frontal rainfall.

In the last 24 hours, the highest gauge total in England and Wales was 7.0mm at Bethesda Quarry Raingauge in Gwynedd, with 2.7mm at Kinsford Gate in Devon and 2.5mm at Brotherswater in Cumbria; no gauges recorded over 10mm in 1 hour. Antecedent rainfall was more notable earlier this week, especially across parts of southeast and east England on Monday and Tuesday and more widely on Sunday, while the only active rainfall-related warning is the Met Office Yellow thunderstorm warning for South West England this evening; no named storm is involved.

UKV (run Wed 24/2200 BST) gives only around 0.7mm area-mean across the South West up to late tonight (Thu 25/2200 BST), with county means peaking near 2.1mm in Plymouth and 1.4mm in Devon and Cornwall. Into tomorrow, UKV (run Wed 24/2200 BST) shows the wettest England and Wales region as the West Midlands with 2.5mm by late Friday (Fri 26/2200 BST), with county means up to 8.3mm in Stoke-on-Trent, 5.6mm in Blackburn with Darwen, 4.9mm in Greater Manchester and 3.9mm in Blaenau Gwent; flood risk remains VERY LOW overall, with only isolated LOW surface water impacts possible if thunderstorms affect the South West later today.

- "headline": One sentence, max 12 words.

    Para 1 — Synoptic scene: describe what the MSLP charts show and how the pattern has changed; name the feature driving the weather (front, low, ridge etc).
    Para 2 — Recent observations: where the heaviest rain fell in the last 24h with gauge point-totals and region names; note antecedent context from the daily accumulation maps and any active Met Office warnings (naming any storm).

Rainfall thresholds: 10mm/1h heavy; 30mm/1h extreme; 100mm/24h exceptional.

Style: professional third-person prose; no bullet points; specific place names and mm values. Gauge values are single-site point totals; UKV values are spatial area-means — keep these distinct. Only mention meteorological mechanisms (orographic enhancement, frontal lifting, convective instability, etc.) where the radar imagery, gauge distribution, or MSLP charts specifically support it — do not assert mechanisms without evidence. Say flood risk once, proportionately, at the end. In quiet conditions say so plainly.
